`integration/docs_artifact_counts_test.go` asks the same questions from the CLI suite's directory. The
duplication is deliberate: a guard that lives only in the package the agent did not run is a guard that did not
run (ADR 0313's shard lesson and ADR 0317's cache lesson, both saying the verifier has to be in the gate that
gets gated). The row locator keys on the **full artifact path**, not the basename — `pkg/lang/testdata/
interpreter-golden-drift.json` and `integration/testdata/interpreter-golden-drift.json` share a basename, and a
guard that finds the first of the two would certify the second by a file it never read.

**Counting is not just `len`.** The record is counted twice, from two decodings that must agree: the map decode
the suite reads it with, and a token-stream walk of the `entries` object that keeps duplicates. A JSON document
with one source spelled twice decodes cleanly and silently keeps the last of the pair, so the record would
report a number of entries the loader cannot reach. The same file is the one `tools/recmerge` appends to, and an
append is exactly how a repeated key arrives.

**Verified against its own ability to fail.** `TestTheCountGuardCanFail` doctors each of the four table rows in
memory (bumps the count by one, requires the row to be a unique slice of the document first) and requires the
guard to report the disagreement — and the guard was run red for real by editing `docs/operations.md` to 5947
and `AGENTS.md` to 5900 and reading the two failures, which name the file, the artifact, both numbers, and the
cell to edit. A guard nobody has watched fail is a comment with a `Test` prefix.

**Counts that stay in prose are counts that rot.** Three sentences in this cycle's own artifacts carried a
literal record size for rhetorical effect (`a 2300-line reformatting of 5913 entries`, `a record whose 5900
entries are re-sorted`, `re-marshalling 5913 entries`). All three were rewritten to say the same thing without a
number, because none of them is a claim anyone can check later; where a count matters it is the table's, and the
table is computed. `_001_session_learnings.md` keeps its dated figures — it is a journal, and "the record was
5913 when this was measured" is a fact that does not change.

**The same test pointed at the tracker.** Having written the artifact-count guard, the natural question was what
else in the tree claims a number about a file without opening it. `roadmap.md`'s Snapshot table — the one a
reader consults first, and the one captioned **"(measured, not remembered)"** — failed eight of its own
assertions on the first run of `pkg/lang/roadmap_snapshot_test.go`:

| Row | It said | The artifact says | How it got that way |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ADRs` | 306 records, highest `0314` | 311 records, highest `0319` | rotted: five ADRs landed since the count was taken |
| `Retired-engine record` | 5913 sources | 5948 | rotted: this cycle's 35 additions |
| `Rows owed` | 101 of 117 queue rows | 101 of 119 | rotted: three rows added when Gap R.197 closed |
| `Matrix rows` | 174 → 135 asserted + 39 divergent | 174 → 136 + 38 | **moved by this cycle's own work** — promoting `probe_a_fold_orders_two_built_containers.gy` out of debt flips a row from divergent to conformant |
| `Oracle verdicts` | 120 `match` · 33 `debt` · 21 n/a | 121 · 32 · 21 | the same promotion, seen from the other column |
| `Test suite` | `go test -tags=llvm20 ./...` | the gate is `-count=1` | the tracker never absorbed ADR 0317 |

The middle two are the important ones. Nobody forgot to update them: closing Gap R.197 *caused* them to become
wrong, in the honest course of doing the work, and no step in that cycle's checklist — roadmap row, details, ADR,
both legs, docs — could have caught it. A summary table that changes value as a side effect of unrelated merges
is exactly the thing a test has to own. The last row is the same defect wearing prose: an agent that copies the
test command out of the tracker gets the cached gate ADR 0317 removed, which is how a documented rule becomes a
rule half the contributors have read.

**How the guard reads a table without becoming the table.** Rows are matched by their label cell ("Matrix rows"),
not by position, and only the value cell is read — so renaming a row fails as `no "Matrix rows" row` rather than
silently passing, and the "Measured by" column can hold filenames, commit hashes and timeouts without smuggling
digits into a comparison. Each row declares how many integers its cell should contain and what they must equal,
computed from the artifact at run time; a row whose wording drifts to a different number of digits fails with
both lists printed, and the message says to fix the guard's reading, not the roadmap's claim. The queue count is
the one row whose artifact is the tracker itself: it counts the Open queue's rows (and the non-`DONE` ones) from
the table, which is also what makes "the open queue is the only list of owed work" a checkable statement rather
than an aspiration.

<a id="gap-r-205"></a>
### Gap R.205 — an Evidence cell cited two test files that are not in the tree, and a `DONE` row nobody could falsify (CLOSED by ADR 0320, owner `tooling`)

**Measured immediately after Gap R.204.** Having written a guard over the tracker's counts, the obvious next
question was what else the tracker asserts that nothing reads. `roadmap.md`'s Evidence cells are the answer:
they are the reason a `Status` cell means anything, and the tracker's own column contract says the Status cell is
the authority *because* the evidence behind it can be gone and looked at. `Gap R.189` — the `KeyError` row, 🟨
`PARTIAL` — cited

```
pkg/lang/key_error_message_test.go            (no such file)
integration/key_error_names_the_key_test.go   (no such file)
```

Neither exists. ADR 0301's cycle wrote those names; a later refactor folded the cases into
`container_methods_test.go` as `TestKeyErrorNamesTheKey` and `TestCLIKeyErrorNamesTheKeyOnTheLegThatCan`; the
code kept being tested, the cell kept citing a tree that no longer had those files, and the row stayed 🟨.

**Why no mechanism caught it.** A test that does not exist cannot fail. `go test -run TestKeyErrorNamesTheKey`
is a green no-op when the name matches nothing, and the full-suite runs that certified this cycle green were
running the *renamed* cases under their new names — the behaviour was covered, only the citation was dead. The
tracker is read by agents as an index of what is proven; a dead citation converts "proven" into "asserted", and
the failure is invisible precisely because the suite is honest.

**The guard, and why its exemption is a data file.** `pkg/lang/roadmap_evidence_test.go` walks every line of
`roadmap.md` and requires each backticked repository path to exist, and each `path::TestName` to find
`func TestName` inside the file it names. Files under `pkg/`, `integration/`, `cmd/`, `tools/`, `docs/` are
matched; a citation may be exempted only if the path is a **known-deleted artifact** — read from
`testdata/witness-banned-phrases.txt`, the ledger the witness guard already keeps, which contains `pkg/lang/jit.go`,
`EvalExpr`, `EvalProgram`, `InterpreterRun`. That ledger is the right exemption because it is *data about
deletions*: a line may cite a deleted file in order to say it stayed deleted, and Gap R.190's row does exactly
that. A renamed test file is a different thing: not a deletion anyone recorded, and a rename is not history that
deserves a licence. The tempting alternative — exempt any line carrying a history marker from
`witness-history-markers.txt` — was measured and rejected: it licences *almost every long row*, because a
300-word row almost always contains `was`, `before`, `recorded`, or `the record`. Measured: with the marker
exemption, **0 of the 3 dead citations** were caught; with the deletion ledger, all 3.

**The other half of the fix is a rule for refactors.** The guard makes a dead citation loud the next time the
suite runs; the reason it was born is that refactors move cases between files as a matter of course. The row's
failure text says the rule: *when a refactor moves a case into another file, the refactor edits the cell that
cited it.* That sentence exists so the next cycle has something to obey rather than rediscover.

**Verified against its own ability to fail, twice.** `TestTheCitationGuardCanFail` is four table cases over a
fabricated row: a file that is not there, a `::TestName` the file does not hold, a retired artifact that must be
exempt, and a real file + real case that must resolve — each failure required to name the row it came from. And
the whole guard was run red for real by restoring the two dead citations and reading the report:

```
Gap R.189: `pkg/lang/key_error_message_test.go` — no such file
Gap R.189: `integration/key_error_names_the_key_test.go` — no such file
```

**What is deliberately not policed.** `docs/roadmap-details.md` and `docs/adr/*` keep their dead paths. Those
files are the measurement narrative and the decision record: they name `pkg/lang/jit.go` in order to explain a
deletion, and an accepted ADR is a historical document — rewriting it to chase a rename destroys the very thing
it is kept for. `integration/docs_citations_test.go` already polices `.gy` citations in the agent-read documents,
and `(planned)` remains the one spelling that may cite a file that does not exist yet.

### L11.6 — numeric truth in the compiled backend: the battery measured, and the clause no leg could reach (CLOSED by ADR 0321, owner L11.1)

The row opened as "closes Gaps P.1 + P.2" and spent nine ADRs acquiring strikethroughs. By the time this cycle
started every named defect in it was `DONE` — `/=` (ADR 0274), the float parameter (ADR 0276), the return word
read off the body (ADR 0254), the `round` tie rule (ADR 0236), `round(x, ndigits)` (ADR 0263), `floor`/`ceil`
answering an `int` (ADR 0264), the typed stdlib constant (ADR 0272) — and the row still read 🟨 `PARTIAL`, with a
free-text cell still claiming `print(math.PI)` prints `3` compiled, stale since ADR 0272.

**A row is not closed by its ledger, so the battery was run.** Twenty-one programs, one per clause the row ever
owned, each asked of CPython and of the shipped CLI, comparing stdout bytes and exit codes together:

| clause | program | CPython | compiled |
|---|---|---|---|
| ADR 0216 | `print(-7 // 2)` | `-4` | `-4` |
| ADR 0216 | `print(-3.5 % 2.0)` | `0.5` | `0.5` |
| ADR 0274 | `x = 8` / `x /= 2` | `4.0` | `4.0` |
| ADR 0274 | `t = 0` / `t += 1.5` | `1.5` | `1.5` |
| ADR 0276 | `dbl(0.1)` | `0.2` | `0.2` |
| ADR 0276 | `bump(1.5)` | `2.5` | `2.5` |
| ADR 0254 | `addf(1)` | `2.5` | `2.5` |
| ADR 0236 | `round(2.5)`, `round(1.5)` | `2`, `2` | `2`, `2` |
| ADR 0263 | `round(2.345, 2)`, `round(2.675, 2)` | `2.35`, `2.67` | same |
| ADR 0272 | `import math` / `print(math.PI)` | (no `PI`) | `3.141592653589793` |

Nineteen rows matched outright. The other rows are the interesting ones: `floor`/`ceil` and the `math.PI` family
are names CPython's builtins do not have, so the reference leg answers `NameError` for the very programs the row
is about. That is not a failure and not a pass — it is a clause with no witness.

**Why "no witness" was worth a cycle rather than a footnote.** L11.6's Definition of done names
`probe_math_const`, and that program sits in the matrix as `oracle: not_applicable` for its spelling. The twin in
`integration/module_const_test.go` (`class consts: PI = 3.141592653589793`) compares values, which is honest and
useless for the naming question: the twin adopts our spelling instead of testing it. A name the reference cannot
say is a name the reference leg cannot adjudicate, and an unadjudicated surface is where a wrong answer can live
without ever being measured — the exact class ADR 0319 and ADR 0320 were about, one level out: a claim about
something no test opens.

**The fix is one line per constant, and the direction is the decision.** `stdlib/math.gy` declares the reference's
spellings as the literals and this language's upper-case names as aliases (`PI = pi`), rather than renaming `PI`
away. Renaming would have voided the record entries (`import math` / `print(math.PI)` is on record), the docs and
every corpus program that uses the documented name — a compatibility break smuggled in as a conformance fix. With
the alias, `import math` / `print(math.pi)` *is* a CPython program, the reference leg runs it, and the promoted
row asserts: `probe_math_constant_answers_the_references_spelling.gy` in `conformanceStandalone()`, matrix row
`asserted: true`, `oracle: match`, twelve lines identical byte for byte, including `math.pi // 2` → `1.0`,
`math.pi % 2` → `1.1415926535897931`, `round(math.pi, 2)` → `3.14`, a container of two constants and an f-string
field — the positions that made this row L11.6 rather than a stdlib row.

**The reference's own gaps stayed open.** `math.inf`, `math.nan` and `math.floor(2.7)` all exit 1 today with a
sentence naming what is missing; CPython prints `inf`, `nan`, `2`. They are `Gap R.207` and the unit table pins
the refusals, so paying the row has to move a table. `string.digits` and its five siblings are `Gap R.206`, and
one of them (`PUNCT` vs `punctuation`) differs by more than case — which is why the row names the shape of the fix
(`canonical literal + alias`, and the declaration-shape guard that reads the module's text) rather than just the
desire.

<a id="gap-r-206"></a>
### Gap R.206 — the data modules answer only our spelling of the reference's names (OPEN, measured while closing L11.6, owner L12.x)

`import string` / `print(string.digits)` is `0123456789` in CPython and exits **1** here:

```
gustyc: jit: codegen: unknown module attribute string.digits
```

`stdlib/string.gy` declares `DIGITS`, `LOWERCASE`, `UPPERCASE`, `HEXDIGITS`, `WHITESPACE`, `PUNCT`. Six names, six
references to the same data, none of them spellable by the reference — and `PUNCT` is not even the reference's
word (`punctuation`). The measurement is the one that closed L11.6's stdlib clause: a name the reference cannot
say is a name the reference leg cannot adjudicate, and today the `string` module's whole surface is in that
position. The row is OPEN because the fix is a decision already made (ADR 0321's `pi` literal + `PI` alias, plus
the declaration-shape guard that reads the module's text and refuses a duplicated literal), applied to a second
module, with a probe the reference can run: five declarations, one program, and `tools/recmerge` for the record.
What must not happen is the `string` module acquiring lower-case names by a different mechanism (a checker alias,
a fallback lookup) — the module is data, and the compiler should not be saying what a data file can say.

<a id="gap-r-207"></a>
### Gap R.207 — three members of the reference's `math` module are absent (OPEN, measured while closing L11.6, owner codegen)

| program | CPython | compiled today |
|---|---|---|
| `print(math.inf)` | `inf` | exit 1 — `unknown module attribute math.inf` |
| `print(math.nan)` | `nan` | exit 1 — the same sentence |
| `print(math.floor(2.7))` | `2` | exit 1 — `string-method floor on a receiver that is not a text the compiler can read: math` (Gap I.2, ADR 0166) |

Three refusals in words, none a wrong answer at exit 0, and none of them this cycle's answer. They stayed separate
for a reason worth keeping: `inf` and `nan` are not literals this language's number lexer accepts (Gap R.135 owns
the exponent half of that lexer), so a data module cannot simply declare them — the emitter's float spelling has
to be involved, which is a codegen change and not a stdlib edit. And `math.floor` is a *call* through a module
receiver, which is the string-method road's Gap I.2 limitation, not a constant's. Bundling either into the naming
cycle would have put two semantics decisions and a lexer dependency inside an ADR about a name, and the row that
pays them should be the one that says which of the three roads it took.

The refusals are pinned in `pkg/lang/math_const_spelling_test.go::TestAMathNameTheModuleDoesNotDeclareIsRefusedInWords`
— `math.PI2`, `math.pi_`, `math.inf`, `math.nan` — so the row cannot be "fixed" by a change that makes one of them
answer something plausible; paying it means editing that table on purpose.

<a id="gap-r-208"></a>
### Gap R.208 — the tracker's `[record]` links point at anchors that are not in the file they point at (OPEN, measured while closing L11.6, owner docs)

ADR 0320 made an Evidence cell's backticked paths resolve. Its neighbouring claim — the `[record](…#anchor)` link
that is supposed to carry a row's measurement — was not covered, and it is in worse shape: `roadmap.md` holds 284
links into `docs/roadmap-details.md`, 266 distinct fragments, and **68 of them name an `<a id="…">` that file does
not have**. 67 sit above a heading that exists and merely never got the anchor the file's own convention requires
for the other 233 anchors in that file — 63 short `gap-r-N` fragments that were never written, plus 5 long-form
`gap-r186--an-f-strings-…` fragments, which are a different mistake: written as if a heading slug had been pasted
in by hand. One — `gap-r-126` — has no section to land on at all.

The consequence is not cosmetic in the way a broken link on a blog is. The `[record]` link is how a row's *why*
reaches a reader who is deciding whether to trust a `DONE`: follow it today and you get the top of a 9,500-line
document and a browser's find bar. For an agent the same link is the difference between reading the measurement and
guessing from the Status cell — and the Status cell is exactly what the measurement exists to check.

Reproducing the count is two commands, which is why the row carries the numbers rather than a vibes estimate:

```
grep -o 'roadmap-details\.md#[a-z0-9-]*' roadmap.md            | sort -u   # the claims
grep -o '<a id="[^"]*"' docs/roadmap-details.md | sed 's/.*id="//;s/"//' | sort -u   # the witnesses
```

Two repairs from this cycle are already in, both found because they affected a number this file publishes:

* **the five anchors this cycle's own rows needed** — `gap-r-203` … `gap-r-207`. A cycle that files a row and links
  it must land the link; leaving it dead while writing "measured, not remembered" two tables earlier is the shape
  this row exists to refuse.
* **the Open queue's split table**. The queue is one markdown table, and the scanner that computes "Rows owed" stops
  at the first line that is not a row. A blank line had been committed inside it, so the four rows filed under it
  (Gap R.202, R.203, R.206, R.207) were owed work that the published tally did not count: the Snapshot said
  `101 of 119` while the file held 123 rows and 104 owed them. The blank line is gone, and
  `pkg/lang/roadmap_snapshot_test.go` now counts those rows *and* fails the run when it sees the split
  (`TestTheQueueCounterSeesWhatASplitTableHides`, verified red by re-splitting the table in a string — the counter
  without the look-ahead reports 121 total / 102 owed, which is the lie this guards).

Rejected: fixing all 68 in this cycle (67 of them are one line each above an existing heading, but `gap-r-126`'s
missing section is a piece of writing that has to be written, and 67 mechanical edits in a commit about a stdlib
name would make both changes harder to review); trusting GitHub's generated heading slugs instead of the file's
explicit `<a id>` convention (the convention already covers 233 entries and is greppable — a slug rule that has to
be re-derived from a renderer is how the long-form fragments went wrong in the first place).

<a id="gap-r-191"></a>
### Gap R.191 — a container that holds a text closed another container's number door (CLOSED by ADR 0322, owner L11.1)

The row was filed as a mis-firing refusal, and that is what the measurement says it was. Three binaries, one
program:

| program | CPython | compiled before ADR 0322 | compiled after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `w = []` / `w.append("a")` / `nested = []` / `nested.append([7, 8])` / `d = nested[0][0] * 2` / `print([d])` | `[14]` | exit 1 — `index cannot reach into nested's slots: the name was rebound, mutated, or handed to code this pass cannot see …` | `[14]` |
| the same without the binding line, `print(nested[0][0] * 2)` | `14` | exit 1, the same sentence | `14` |
| `w.append("a")` / `xs.append([7.5, 8])` / `print(xs[0][0] * 2)` | `15.0` | exit 1 | `15.0` |
| `w.append("a")` / `d = {}` / `d["k"] = 40` / `print(d["k"] + 2)` | `42` | exit 1 | `42` |
| `w.append("a")` / `outer.append([[7, 8]])` / `print(outer[0][0][0] + 1)` | `8` | exit 1 | `8` |
| `xs.append([7, 8])` / `ys = xs` / `ys.append("word")` / `print(xs[1] * 2)` | `wordword` | exit 1 | exit 1 — the block crossed the alias |

The row's own observation was the diagnosis: drop the two `w` lines and the program answered. What was dropped
was not a mutation of `nested` — it was the flag. `numericSlotChains`, the pass that decides whether `+` and `*`
over a slot the literal no longer describes may be lowered at all, carried `blocked bool`: one text, or one value
with no spelling, written into *any* container anywhere set it, and the door closed for the module. The pass is
coarse on purpose — the reference *answers* `xs[0] + "a"` with a joined text and `[1] * 2` with a repeated list,
neither of which this backend builds from a slot (`Gap R.82`), so a door that opened on a container holding a
text would raise where the reference returns a value. Coarse is defensible when it only ever refuses more. What
made this a defect rather than a hedge is that a refusal is a *sentence*: the message named `nested`, the
container the read walks, as the thing that had been "rebound, mutated, or handed to code this pass cannot see",
and the line responsible was two statements earlier and about a different object.

**The fix is a key, not a widening.** `blocked` became a map keyed by an alias group's root; the walk builds the
groups (`y = xs`, `a, b = xs`, `d = xs[0]`, `for v in xs`, `[v for v in xs]`, and a call site linking each
parameter to the argument that reaches it), and a store blocks the container it writes plus everyone who can
denote it. Evidence — the per-name kind tree `numeric` reads — stays per-name, so an alias can only ever close a
door, never open one: `xs.append([7,8])` / `ys = xs` / `ys.append([9,10])` still proves nothing about `xs`. The
program-wide bit survives as `blockAll` for the stores that describe no name at all (`xs[0].append("a")`,
`self.items.add(b)`, a loop variable over `rows()`), which is the only case where "which container?" genuinely
has no answer.

**Two holes in the same walk closed while it was being re-read.** `xs += ["a"]` extends a container without ever
naming it as a receiver, and `xs[0][1] = "a"` writes a slot two levels down for which the notebook has no level;
neither was recorded before, so neither blocked anything. Both do now — the second blocks the program, since the
object it writes is one the pass cannot point at. `Comp`, `Generator`, `Slice`, `Lambda`, `AssignExpr`, `WithStmt`,
`MatchStmt`, `ClassDef`, `YieldStmt` and `YieldFromStmt` joined the walk for the same reason: a store the pass
does not visit is a store that cannot block anything.

**The table that was supposed to keep this honest had been answering nothing.** `TestNumericSlotChainGate` — the
"gate asked directly, so a widening of `+` fails a decision row" table — took the print argument and handed it to
`chainDepth`, which reports no chain for anything but a bare subscript. Every row is written
`print(xs[0][0] + 1)`; every row therefore reached `t.Skip("row has no print(...) argument to walk")`. The one
existing row whose expected value this cycle inverted — `"text anywhere in any container"` → closed — had never
run. `gateChain` now walks `BinOp`/`UnOp`/`CondExpr`/call arguments to find the read, and a row that yields no
chain is a failure rather than a skip (the ADR 0317 lesson, met from the inside this time: a guard over a file it
never opened is not a guard).

Witnesses: `pkg/lang/numeric_slot_door_scope_test.go` (ten answering programs on the record leg and the compiled
run; fourteen rows asking the pass directly, including the alias, the loop variable, the parameter, the unknown
callee and the two stores the old walk missed; `TestTheAliasGuardCanFail`, which builds the notebook with the
union-find removed and demands the alias row change verdict; the still-refusing family with its sentences),
`integration/numeric_slot_door_scope_test.go` (the same answering family against CPython, the still-shut family
pinned as refusals, and `TestCLIAgentTheDoorScopeRowsThatBelongToAnotherRowAreFiledNotFixed` for the two refusals
measured beside this one that belong to `Gap R.101` and the loop-variable rows `Gap R.91`/`R.95`), and
`integration/programs/probe_a_text_in_one_container_leaves_another_number_door_open.gy`, promoted into the
conformance corpus and recorded through `tools/recmerge` (the reference's answer, cross-checked against the
compiled leg). A 187-program differential across `integration/programs/*.gy` between the pre-cycle build and this
one differs on that file alone.

### Gap R.95 — the membership test and the loop chose their helper by the kind the compiler had written down (CLOSED by ADR 0323, owner L11.1)

The row was filed as two refusals. Measured again on the day it closed, one of them was not a refusal at
all, and the thing it was instead is the reason this cycle exists.

| program | CPython | compiled before ADR 0323 | compiled after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `xs = []` / `xs.append([7, 8])` / `print(7 in xs[0])` | `True` | exit 1, `this context needs a single static kind` | `True` |
| `xs = []` / `xs.append([7, 8])` / `for v in xs[0]: print(v)` | `7`, `8` | exit 1, same sentence | `7`, `8` |
| `d = {}` / `d["a"] = [1, 2]` / `for v in d["a"]: print(v)` | `1`, `2` | **`0` at exit 0** | `1`, `2` |
| `d = {}` / `d["a"] = "abc"` / `for v in d["a"]: print(v)` | `a`, `b`, `c` | **nothing at exit 0** | `a`, `b`, `c` |
| `xs = []` / `xs.append(5)` / `print(1 in xs[0])` | `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` | **`False` at exit 0** | the raise, catchable |
| `xs = []` / `xs.append(5)` / `for v in xs[0]: print(v)` | `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` | **`0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` at exit 0** — five iterations invented from a heap slot | the raise, catchable |

Measured with three binaries the same afternoon: CPython 3.12, the HEAD build, this cycle's build. The two
refusals print the whole ADR 0249 sentence (`a compiled list holds elements of more than one kind … this
context needs a single static kind (roadmap L11.1, Gap R.82)`) and exit 1; the table abbreviates.

The refusals were admissible: a door that cannot see far enough says so. The other four were not. Each
answered, at the exit code of success, with a word the program never computed — and each of them did it in
exactly the shapes where the compiler *had* written a kind down. `d` is a runtime dict, so the loop asked
`rt_dict_len` of the dict and walked the dict's own words, one entry deep, over a value that had never been a
dict's entry at all. The membership test lowered `xs[0]` through the value path, got a payload that was an
integer, handed it to `rt_contains` as a heap handle, and read whatever object happened to share the number 5.

**The root cause was one line's worth of bookkeeping, in two copies.** Both callers select a runtime helper,
and both selected it from `g.runtimeDicts` / `g.listVars` / `g.mixedLists` — the notebook of what the *container
variable* is — where the haystack is a *slot*, whose kind is a fact about the object and was recorded beside
the payload by whoever wrote it. ADR 0251 had already solved this exact problem for the read one level below
such a slot: `slotReadUnderTag` emits one `icmp`/`br` per kind and asks `rt_get_elem`, `rt_dict_get_tagged`,
`rt_str_char` or `rt_set_find` in the arm the tag selects, with the raise arms leaving through the program's
own `except`. The two callers had never been given the door.

**What landed is that door, handed over, not a new one.** `builtSlotPair` reads the slot the only way a slot
can be read when nothing describes it — `rt_get_elem`/`rt_tag_of` or `rt_dict_get_tagged`/`rt_dict_value_tag`,
which is ADR 0187's pairing rule, and it declines the shape ADR 0241's static door already serves so the two
never compete. `membershipOfBuiltSlotHaystack` then walks the tag: `@rt_contains_tagged` for a list,
`@rt_dict_has_tagged` for a dict (its keys, because that is what Python tests a dict by), `@rt_set_contains_tagged`
for a set, and `@rt_str_contains` for a text — a different question in the last arm, and one the arm can only
ask of a needle whose kind is provable, which is ADR 0232's rule kept whole: a needle the compiler cannot
describe declines, and the old refusal stands rather than comparing an `@str_tab` index with the integer it is
indexed by. The loop asks the object three questions through `@rt_iter_len`, `@rt_iter_elem` and `@rt_iter_tag`,
which live in the same runtime block as the helpers they call — a list yields elements, a set members, a dict
its keys at the stride 2 the dict's own reader walks, a text its characters, interned and tagged `str` so the
loop variable prints as text and not as the index of it (ADR 0225, ADR 0185).

**Iterability is a raise, not a refusal, and the two questions do not share a sentence.** CPython says
`argument of type 'int' is not iterable` to a membership test and `'int' object is not iterable` to a loop.
Those are not stylistic variants and the door keeps them apart, one arm per kind, each leaving through
`raiseTo` so an `except TypeError:` in the source reaches it (ADR 0228) — the same discipline ADR 0271 learned
when `abs` borrowed the unary minus's wording. A text haystack asked about a number raises the third sentence,
`'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int`, naming the *needle's* kind. The `@rt_iter_*` helpers
never raise: they are reached only from an arm that already proved the kind iterable, which keeps the source
span, the exception class and the handler stack where the compiler can see them.

**Two things this cycle measured and did not fix.** A haystack *two slots* deep still refuses — reaching it is
dispatching a dispatch, and the honest answer is the sentence that names the missing half (`Gap R.210`). And a
slot holding an instance of a user class carries the `int` tag, so `print(xs[0])` of a slot appended with `C()`
prints the heap handle, `len(xs[0])` names `'int'`, and the two new doors name `'int'` where the reference names
the class (`Gap R.209`). The second is the same missing word Gap R.112 found for a verdict in a slot, and it is
a writer's bug rather than a reader's: an arm that guessed the class would be inventing an object it cannot see.

Witnesses: `pkg/lang/runtime_slot_read_test.go` grows the parity table (31 programs judged against the record and
against the compiled run, including one container holding a list, a dict, a set and a text at once so all four
arms run in one module, the loop surface of `break`/`continue`/`else` over a slot, and the static door's shapes
kept so the new door cannot disturb them), the trap table (13 raises compared by class **and** message with the
record, each then caught by the source's own handler), and the IR table (the module branches on the tag, asks one
helper per kind, carries each raise's own sentence — and a loop the compiler *can* describe carries none of the
three doors). `integration/runtime_slot_read_test.go` grows 22 CLI rows byte-compared with CPython — one more moved
in from the trap table once it became catchable — with 9 traps pinned
at exit 3 and exit 2 forbidden, the two depth-two refusals pinned at exit 1, and the filed instance row — one for
the test and one for the loop.
`integration/programs/runtime_slot_haystack.gy` joined the conformance corpus as `match`, and 57 sources went to
the record through `tools/recmerge` (5972 → 6029, 0 dropped / 0 changed). One row left the compiled-vs-record

out of a comprehension-built list, recorded as "the compiled backend cannot build a program the engine ran" —
which is the `@rt_set_contains_tagged` arm arriving from the other direction (338 → 337).

### Gap R.209 — an instance written into a container slot carries the `int` tag (CLOSED by ADR 0325, found by ADR 0323)

`xs = []` / `xs.append(C())` / `print(xs[0])` printed `1` — the heap handle — where the reference prints
`<__main__.C object at 0x…>`. `len(xs[0])` raised `object of type 'int' has no len()`. Asking the slot for a
membership test or a loop, which is what ADR 0323 added, raised `argument of type 'int' is not iterable` and
`'int' object is not iterable` where the reference names the class.

One cause, four symptoms: the tag the *writer* left beside the payload says int. Everything downstream —
the printer, the length check, the ordering sentence, and the two doors ADR 0323 added — obeys the tag,
which is the rule ADR 0182 and ADR 0187 exist to enforce, so the bug is not in any of them. `elemKindTag` is the
one place the answer is written, and it already had the table to read: `negation.go`'s `signlessOperandKind`
names `Token` for `-Token()` and `abs(Token())` (ADR 0271), so the class of a construction is knowable at the
write site. ADR 0259 is the precedent — a bool in a slot went from `TagInt` to `TagBool` and the container
printer, the set dedup and the ordering sentence followed without being touched.

**Closed on the ADR 0259 pattern.** `elemKindTag` now admits a bare constructor call or a name whose latest
binding the assignment walk knows to be an instance, and returns `TagInstance`. The payload remains the heap
handle. The class name is not copied into the slot: the constructor already wrote the dispatch id into object
slot 0, and the module's class table reads it. `@rt_class_qual` supplies `__main__.C` to the identity form,
`@rt_class_short` supplies `C` to the five TypeError sentences, and `@rt_instance_msg_ptr` formats only the
selected sentence while the compiler arm owns the code, span and landing pad. The four symptoms follow because
the four readers were already obedient; none of them was asked to guess.

The second measurement was the static binary road. `c in "abc"` had answered `True`, and `"abc" in c` had
answered `False`, at exit 0, before either arm consulted the object's tag. Membership of a text takes a text
needle, and membership of an instance is a raise against the haystack; the two sentences name different sides
of the operation. Those arms now raise before the substring or container road can turn a reference TypeError
into a verdict.

A CPython address is an allocation accident, not a semantic claim. The compiled backend prints the object's
heap slot in the same position, and the oracle's narrow `instance-identity` rule normalizes only the complete
identity form on both legs to `0x…`. The class inside the brackets is still compared byte for byte, and the CLI
row explicitly rejects output that is merely a number.

The filed pin `TestASlotHoldingAnInstanceNamesTheWrongKindForMembershipAndLoop` is gone. In its place, the
parity and trap tables answer the old wrong answers directly: 6 CLI traps and 6 CLI identity-print rows, plus
the unit class-runtime, identity-containment and negative-control tables. `runtime_slot_instance_tag.gy` joined

That is not an inconsistency in the answer — both refusals name the half they are missing, and exit 1 is the

Pinned by the two `…_two_slots_deep` rows in `pkg/lang/runtime_slot_read_test.go::TestRunTimeBuiltNestedSlotReadRefusesWhatItCannotProve`

**Closed the way the row said it would be.** `builtSlotPair` asked `containerHandleOf` for the side the slot is

### Gap R.211 — the door reached the haystack and read the needle off a notebook (CLOSED by ADR 0324, found by ADR 0324)

This row is ADR 0323's own defect, found the afternoon after it shipped by asking the door the questions the row
had not asked. Two shapes, both answering at the exit code of success where the reference answers something else:

| program | CPython | ADR 0323 | after ADR 0324 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `xs.append([{"k": 1}])` / `d["z"] = {"k": 1}` / `print(d["z"] in xs[0])` | `True` | **`False` at exit 0** | `True` |
| `xs.append([1, 2])` / `ys.append([1, 2])` / `print(ys[0] in xs[0])` | `True` | refused (`…needs a single static kind`) | `True` |
| `xs.append({"k": 1})` / `print([1] in xs[0])` | `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` | **`False` at exit 0** | that raise, catchable |
| `xs.append({1, 2})` / `print([1] in xs[0])` | `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` | **`False` at exit 0** | that raise, catchable |
| `xs.append({1, 2})` / `ys.append({1})` / `print(ys[0] in xs[0])` | `False` | `False` | `False` — and it must stay `False` |

The first two are one bug: a needle that is itself a slot read took its kind from `g.runtimeDicts` /
`g.listVars` — the notebook of what the *container variable* is — which describes the container the needle came
out of, not the needle. Two dict literals with the same entries live in two objects, so a comparison keyed on the
payload answered with two addresses, and the reference compares contents. The fix is the one the haystack already
used: ask the object (`builtSlotPair` for a needle that is an `Index`), and let `rt_payload_eq`'s container arm
recurse.

The next two are the same family one step over: a dict is looked up by its key and a set is hashed by its member,
and a container can be neither. Reporting "not present" loses an entire error class — the program's
`except TypeError:` has nothing to catch — so the arm asks one question per container kind of the **needle's tag**
and raises `unhashable type: 'list'` / `'dict'` / `'set'`. The tag, not the compiler's proven kind, for the reason
this whole file keeps repeating: a slot's kind is a fact about the object.

The last row is the reason the guard is keyed by tag rather than by a blanket "no containers". `{1} in {1, 2}` is
`False` in the reference, not a `TypeError`: a set needle asked of a set is converted to the frozenset it hashes
as. This language has no frozenset to find, so the answer is a well-behaved "not found" — and the row is pinned so
the day someone adds frozensets finds out which assumption it was resting on. ADR 0311 is the precedent two commits
up the road: an unhashable *write* raises from its tag; this is the read.

### Gap R.212 — a needle whose kind cannot be proven has no arm (OPEN, found by ADR 0324)

`def pick(v):` returning a number on one path and a text on another, `xs.append([7, 8])`, then
`print(1 if pick(0) in xs[0] else 0)`: `0` in the reference, exit 1 compiled, with the mixed-list sentence naming
what it cannot describe.

This is not the depth problem (Gap R.210, closed) or the notebook problem (Gap R.211, closed). The haystack's tag
picks the arm, and the arm compares the needle's payload against each slot **under a tag**; a call's answer has no
tag in this backend yet, so there is no operand to compare and no arm that could be trusted. Guessing the kind
would return whichever verdict happened to match the number in the slot, which is the class of bug this file has
been writing against since ADR 0233. The refusal is the honest answer, and it is pinned as one: exit 1, the
sentence checked, and no IR problem hiding behind it.

The missing half is already built for a different door: ADR 0273's callee returns the pair (`@rt_call_tagged`'s
third return road), which is what lets `print(twice(xs[0][0]))` print `14`. Hand that pair to `taggedOperand` for
a call operand and this row moves to the parity tables; until then it is Gap R.83's unprovable operand, seen from
the membership door instead of the equality door.

### Gap R.37 — the constant fold refused, or answered, what the reference raises (CLOSED by ADR 0326)

The trap machinery was finished long before this row was paid. ADR 0211 gave every built-in trap a class,
ADR 0181 gave the raise a frame-closing unwind, ADR 0166 fixed what each exit code means — and there was a
second place a trap got decided that none of them had visited: the **constant fold**. When a subscript's base
was something the compiler could read — a literal list, a literal text, a literal dict, a comprehension's
object, a function that hands back a literal — five roads asked themselves what to do with a position that did
not fit, and all five answered the same way: a `codegen:` refusal, at `gustyc`'s exit 1.

The comparison that makes that a defect rather than a limitation is not "refusal versus a correct answer", it
is "refusal versus **the reference**". The reference does not refuse. `print([][0])` prints a traceback; a
`try:` around it is legal, and the `except IndexError:` runs. The compiler was converting a fact about a value
at the moment it is read into a verdict about the whole program, delivered before the program had executed
anything — and taking the `except` with it, which is not cosmetic: wrapping the read is how a person finds out
which index was wrong.

The half that made the row urgent was the conversions, because those had not refused — they had been *widened*,
which is how a wrong answer ships:

| program | what the fold did | what the reference says |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| `print(float("x"))`, `print(float(" "))` | printed `0.0` (`goErr` swallowed the parse failure and `strconv.ParseFloat("")` returned 0) | `ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'x'` |
| `print(float(None))`, `print(float([1,2]))`, `print(float({"a":1}))`, `print(float({1}))` | printed `0.0` | `TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a real number, not '…'` |
| `print(int("abc"))`, `print(int("1 0"))`, `print(int("0x10"))` | refused: `int on non-integer string` (Gap I.2) | `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'` |
| `print(ord("ab"))`, `print(ord(""))` | printed `97` and `0` — the first byte of a text that is not one character | `TypeError: ord() expected a character, but string of length 2 found` |
| `print(chr(-1))`, `print(chr(1114112))` | built a one-element list of a nonsense code point | `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x110000)` |
| `print(int(True))`, `print(float(True))` | refused: `int expects a number or numeric string` (Gap R.213) | `1` and `1.0` |

One door closes all of it: `constantTrap` is the fold's route to the raise the program would have reached, and
it opens a fresh block behind the raise because `raiseTo` ends the current one — the first build emitted past a
terminator and failed the verifier, which is ADR 0166's exit 2 and the reason the block is part of the door
rather than the caller's problem. The sentences come from the table the *dynamic* road already read
(`listIndexOutOfRange`, `stringIndexOutOfRange`), so paying this row did not create a second wording of one
error; the wording that differs from the reference (`index out of range` vs `list index out of range`) stays
Gap R.90's, for both roads at once, and is why three unit rows assert the two sentences separately — the
recorder refuses to write a record the two legs do not agree on, which is the recorder being right.

Five ledger rows went out as **paid**: `print(int("abc"))`, `print(float("zzz"))`, `s = "abc"; print(s[9])`
and the two `try:/except ValueError:` versions of the first pair — recorded as "the compiled backend cannot
build a program the engine ran" and as "answered 0.0 where the record prints `handled`". The ledger is 337 →
332 and the record is 6095 → 6130, every new entry cross-checked against the compiled leg by `tools/recmerge`.

`int(True)` is `1` in the reference and `codegen: int expects a number or numeric string` at exit 1 here. The
conversion folds had arms for integer literals, float literals, texts and the no-argument forms; the boolean
arm was simply absent, in a language whose `True` is an `int`. Paid in the same door: `int`/`float` take a
`BoolLit` and answer `1`/`0`, `1.0`/`0.0`. Pinned in `TestTheConversionFoldsAnswerRatherThanTrap` and in the
record, because a fold that traps on a *good* literal is as wrong as one that silently answers on a bad one.

### Gap R.215 — a text key into a dict literal refuses while the same key into a dict variable traps (CLOSED by ADR 0327)

```
print({"a": 1}["b"])        # codegen: index must be a constant      (exit 1)  → KeyError: 'b' (exit 3)
print({"a": 1}["a"])        # codegen: index must be a constant      (exit 1)  → 1
d = {"a": 1}
print(d["b"])               # KeyError: 'b'                          (exit 3)  ✅ both before and after
```

A literal is the most constant base there is, and the one road that reads its base statically was the one road
that could not see a text key — the variable road looks the key up and raises. Measured while landing ADR 0326,
and left open rather than bundled; closed the next cycle, and **the root cause was not a missing door**. The
subscript road opens with a gate: a key that is not an `IntLit` is accepted only when the base is a registered
container *name*, and everything else returns `index must be a constant`. The `case *DictLit:` below that gate
was therefore only ever reachable with an integer key, and its helpers (`dictLiteralKeys`, `dictLiteralVals`)
admitted nothing but integer constants — so the fold was not a fast path in front of a general road, it was the
only road, and the sentence `a compiled dict literal holds constant integer keys only; CPython supports string
and other keys` was the backend describing its own gate as a property of the language.

The fix is the gate plus one call: a literal dict whose entries the fold cannot read is built by
`heapDictFrom` — the builder a binding already uses — and read by `taggedSlotPair` against a
`*DictLit` base, which asks `rt_dict_has_tagged` (a miss is the `KeyError` ADR 0326 built, with the key's repr
as its message), `rt_dict_get_tagged` and `rt_dict_value_tag`. The answer is the pair, so the print door, the
`str`/`repr` door, the binding door and the element-position door all take both words; `exprIsString` and
`printsAsInternedStr` answer "is this entry a text?" from the *entry* rather than from a guessed tag. Because the
key is now compared as a value, the literal inherits the dict key rule it always should have had: `1`, `1.0` and
`True` are one key, `True` finds the entry `1` wrote, and a text key is never a number key — `{0: 1}["0"]`
raises where the fold's payload read answered "the key is there".

Two positions stay refusals rather than joining the wrong answers, because they keep one word for a whole value:
`def f(): return {"a": "x"}["a"]` and `g({"a": "x"}["a"])` measured as `1` at **exit 0** under a naive routing —
the text's `@str_tab` index, printed as a number. The refusal names the pair, the one word, and **Gap R.146**,
the row that owns handing a pair across a call. The gate asks whether the entry is a plain integer rather than
trusting `strFuncs`, which is why Gap R.219 is filed beside this row rather than hidden inside it.

Pinned by `pkg/lang/dict_literal_key_test.go` (29 answering rows, 7 missing-key rows with class *and* sentence,
the catchable pair, the fold's negative control, the printer claim, the refusal sentences) and by
`integration/dict_literal_key_test.go` at the CLI against CPython, with `integration/programs/dict_literal_key.gy`
`match`-ing on both legs. The asymmetry the change had to leave behind is Gap R.220.

<a id="gap-r-214"></a>

### Gap R.214 — a subscript of a container handed back by a call is read by the door that reads a variable's slot (CLOSED by ADR 0334)

**Closed 2026-10-14 by ADR 0334**, one cycle after ADR 0333 handed this row the answer it needed. One question
— *read this position out of that list* — was asked of three spellings and got two answers:

```python
def build():
    return [1, 2]

print([1, 2][7])      # IndexError: list index out of range   — the fold's door, since ADR 0326
ys = build()
print(ys[7])          # IndexError: list index out of range   — the variable's door, since ADR 0326
print(build()[7])     # exit 1: codegen: index requires an inline list/dict/set literal
print(build()[0])     # the same refusal, where the reference answers 1
```

**Why it was wrong rather than missing.** Two of the three doors raised the program's own catchable
`IndexError`, with the reference's class, message and exit class; only the third stopped the build with a
compiler sentence. A refusal whose neighbours raise is the asymmetry this tracker prices above a plain
missing feature, and the fold-shaped spelling was the proof: the language already had the trap, the message
and the exit code, so the third line was a door in the wrong place, not an unbuilt room.

**The root cause was a question asked of the wrong fact.** The subscript road chooses its door from the
**spelling of its base** — `*ListLit` to the fold, `*Name` to the variable's read, `*Index` to the object
below — and a `*Call` had no arm, so it fell to `slotReadRefusal`. That was sound while a call handed back
`ret i32 @.lst1` (a global in a value position, which `llc` rejected: the exit-2 defect ADR 0333 exists to
pay for). It stopped being sound the moment ADR 0333 made the answer a heap handle under a rooted name
carrying the notebooks a container variable has. ADR 0251 wrote the same sentence about a container the
program *built*; this is the same misattribution one construct over, which is why the fix is a rewrite and
not a reader: `containerAnswerOperand` lowers the call, the subscript node is **copied** with its base set to
that name, and `ys[i]`'s roads — the kind roads, the mixed reads, the tagged read, ADR 0330's bounds check —
answer. The copy is load-bearing: the same AST node is lowered by more than one road, and an in-place rewrite
would let the second road see a program the first one edited.

**Two traps found while landing it.**

- *Order, not content.* `print(f()[2])` over `{1: "one", 2: "two"}` printed `1` — the value's `@str_tab`
  index — because the tagged door was asked before the kind roads, and a dict built from a **literal** carries
  no per-slot tags, so `rt_dict_get_tagged` answered tag 0, which the printer reads as "int". The bound form
  had always printed `two` because the notebooks are consulted first. The rewrite therefore happens *before*
  every subscript arm of the print door: same roads, same order, or "the same read of the same object" is a
  slogan.
- *A notebook claiming a kind the object outgrew.* `def words(): return ["hi", "ho"]` / `print(words()[1])`
  refused with Gap R.82's "this context needs a single static kind" while `print(xs[1])` of a static literal
  printed `ho` and `print(words())` printed `['hi', 'ho']`. The answer was built **tagged**, and
  `recordContainerAnswer` left `listElemStr` set: the reader took the untagged word road, which has no tag to
  print. The fix is the builder's own rule, copied — a container whose slots describe themselves has no single
  kind, so the element notebooks are cleared (`heapDictFrom`/`heapSetFrom` have always done this for the
  variable they build into; the list half had no variable in hand and nobody did it for it).

**What was deliberately not taken.** The `*Slice` arm of the same judgement. `print(b()[0:2])` refuses today,
and that is the row's decision, recorded so a later cycle does not "finish" it into a wrong answer: the slice
road answers `[1, 0]` for a mixed list and `1` for a bound slice whatever the base is (**Gap R.230**), so
opening it would have converted one honest refusal at exit 1 into two more silently-wrong programs at exit 0.
Two further defects measured on the way out were filed rather than bundled: **Gap R.231** (a number
subscripting a text-keyed dict answers the slot at that position instead of raising `KeyError: 0`, wrong for
every base) and **Gap R.232** (a membership test whose needle is a slot refuses, with a sentence that prints
the needle's Go representation instead of the construct).

**Evidence.** `pkg/lang/container_subscript_test.go` — 36 answered programs whose `want` is CPython's, the
raise rows by class *and* message, the catchable forms, the bound-vs-direct parity runner (`runForParity`),
the fold's negative control over `@main`, `llc` on every module, the filed-not-fixed ledger and the record leg
(`TestTheCallResultSubscriptRowsAreRecorded`). `integration/container_subscript_test.go` runs the same programs
through the CLI against CPython, with the refusals held at exit 1 (empty stdout, no exit 2) and the pair road
witnessed keeping the numeric uses this row did not take. `integration/programs/container_subscript.gy`
(matrix row `programs/container_subscript`, oracle `match`, 26 lines) is the whole door in one program.

### Gap R.217 — a dict read by a container key raises the wrong class (CLOSED by ADR 0328, found by ADR 0327)

**Closed 2026-07-14 by ADR 0328.** A gate asks the program, at each of the three doors that consults
a dict, whether the key is something the language refuses to hash — `pkg/lang/unhashable_key.go`'s

where the reference names the inner type it choked on, so `(1, [2])` says `'list'`; a name the program
last filled with one of them) and the door raises CPython's own sentence, `TypeError: unhashable type:

doors are the subscript read (`checkKeyRead`, `checkKeyReadTagged`) and the store
(`assignIndex`) — the store being the worst of the three, because `d = {}; d[[1]] = 2; print(d)` printed

at exit 0. The gate is asked only of a haystack that hashes its needle: `haystackHashesKeys` keeps it off
a list and a tuple, where membership walks, and `[1] in [[1], [2]]` stays `True` — the direction of wrong
that matters, since a gate that fires too eagerly turns a working program into a raise. The rows are
`pkg/lang/unhashable_key_test.go` (thirteen traps, the soundness table, the classifier and the haystack
asked directly, and the record leg reading `exnType`/`exnMsg` beside the compiled raise) and
`integration/unhashable_key_test.go` (the same doors through the CLI, exit 3 and an empty stdout asserted,
and `integration/programs/unhashable_key.gy` printed line-for-line against CPython). What the row still
does not close is the key whose kind is only a run-time fact — a name the compiler cannot pin to one
container keeps the answer it always gave rather than raise a TypeError it may not deserve, and that is
L11.1's tagged word (ADR 0232's soundness rule). Two neighbours measured on the way are filed beside it:
**Gap R.221** (a dict variable keyed by `None` or a bool reads the wrong entry — the payload road ADR 0327
built a door for and did not finish) and **Gap R.222** (a list or string subscript asked with a key of the
wrong kind answers a number instead of raising `list indices must be integers or slices, not str`).

`print({"a": 1}[[1]])` and `d = {"a": 1}` / `print(d[[1]])` both die with `KeyError: key not found` at exit 3
where the reference raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. A list is not an absent key; it is a key that
cannot be asked. ADR 0324 got this right for a needle into a container *slot*, and `guardHashableTag` stands on

<a id="gap-r-218"></a>
<a id="gap-r-218"></a>
### Gap R.218 — a list literal is read by the door a list's elements are read by (CLOSED by ADR 0331, found by ADR 0327)

The four wrong answers, all at **exit 0**:

| program | the reference | the compiled backend | what the word actually was |
|---|---|---|---|
| `print(["a", "b"][0])` | `a` | `0` | an index into `@str_tab` |
| `print([1.5, 2][0])` | `1.5` | `1` | a `@float_box` handle |
| `print([None, 2][0])` | `None` | `0` | nothing at all |
| `print([True, 2][0])` | `True` | `1` | a bool's 0/1 |

and the rows that were already whole are what made this a defect rather than a missing feature:

| program | the reference | the compiled backend |
|---|---|---|
| `xs = ["a", "b"]` / `print(xs[0])` | `a` | `a` |
| `print([[1, 2], [3, 4]][0])` | `[1, 2]` | `[1, 2]` |
| `print([{"a": 1}][0]["a"])` | `1` | `1` |

**The root cause had a name before the fix, and that is why the fix is one arm.** A subscript has two roads.
The compile-time fold has one word, and reads only a literal of integer constants at an integer position. The
pair door builds the object, writes each element's kind beside its payload as the builder runs, and answers
`(payload, tag)`. `runtimeSlotPairDeep` (`heapargs.go`) *is* that door, and it carried a `*DictLit` arm — ADR
0327's — with nothing list-shaped beside it. A list literal was never admitted, so the fold kept answering
shapes it cannot read.

Four decisions around that arm:

- **The fold keeps exactly what it reads.** `listLiteralFoldAnswers` accepts a literal only when every element
  is an integer constant *and* the position is an integer the literal has. `print([1, 2][0])` still emits a
  constant; the guard is an IR test that fails if it grows an allocation or a call to `rt_print_mixed_value`.
  A gate wider than the fold is how a fix ships a refusal nobody measured (ADR 0249), so the gate is also
  tested as a predicate, away from codegen, with the out-of-range position and the bool position in the table.
- **The door is the variable's door, not a second read.** `listLiteralPair` builds with `containerHandleOf` and
  reads with `containerSlotRead` — the same two calls `xs[i]` emits (`rt_get_elem` beside `rt_tag_of`) — so the
  two roads cannot grow apart, and `TestTheLiteralListRoadIsNeverWorseThanTheVariableRoad` fails the build if
  they do (a row skips only when the *variable* road itself refuses, which is Gap R.82's `xs = [[]]` / `if xs[0]:`).
- **A condition is a pair position, not a one-word position.** The fold used to answer `if [True][0]:` by
  comparing a payload to zero — right for a bool, wrong for the three shapes a tag exists to distinguish:
  `[0.0, 1][0]`, `[[]][0]` and `[""][0]` are falsy in the reference and non-zero words here (a box handle, a
  container handle, an interned index). An `if`, a `while` and a ternary's operand now ask `@rt_pair_truth`,
  the table `and`/`or` already ask. This was not widening for symmetry: the retired engine's own record runs
  `if [True][0]:` / `print("yes")`, so a fix that turned that program into a refusal would have bought a
  ledger row by narrowing the door — a coverage loss dressed as a fix, and the first draft of this cycle did
  exactly that before the ledger caught it.
- **The one-word positions still refuse.** `return ["a","b"][0]`, `id(["a","b"][0])`,
  `print(["a","b"][0] + "!")` and an f-string field name the missing half, the door that does answer it, and
  the two rows that own it (Gap R.218 for the read, Gap R.146 for the position). A wrong answer at exit 0 is
  the failure this row was; refusal is the floor underneath it.

**One gate moved, because widening a door can move a defect through it.** With the literal admitted to the
pair door, `print([1, 2]["a"])` printed whichever slot the text's `@str_tab` index counts to, and
`print(["a", "b"][[0]])` had no word to lower at all — Gap R.222's defect reborn at the new site, caught by
probing the door rather than by the plan. The dict branch of `containerSlotRead` has always asked its own
version of that question *inside* the door (`checkKeyReadTagged`, Gap R.217's unhashable gate); the list
branch now asks its version too (`badIndexGate`), so both halves of the subscript are guarded at the door and
not only on the road that reaches it. `["a","b"][True]` stays legal, because a bool is an int and `True` is
position 1.

Filed rather than bundled, as **Gap R.224**: the same read one layer out — a literal's element that is itself
a literal read — still answers the payload, because the builder's `pairElemPair` admits a `*Name` and not a
subscript.

<a id="gap-r-224"></a>
### Gap R.224 — a literal read placed inside another literal answers the payload (CLOSED by ADR 0332, found by ADR 0331)

```python
print([{"a": "x"}["a"], 2])   # exit 0, prints [1, 2]; the reference prints ['x', 2]
```

ADR 0331's door, one layer out. A container literal builds itself element by element, and each position is
asked for **two** words: a payload, and the tag that says what the payload means. `pairElemPair`
(`heapargs.go`) is the hook that hands over a pair, and it admits exactly one shape — a `*Name` the pair road
bound. A subscript is not a name, so the read is asked for one word, the tag is dropped on the way in, and the
slot ends up holding an `@str_tab` index that the printer is then told to read as a string.

The three twin shapes refuse instead, which is the same door declining rather than lying:

| program | the reference | the compiled backend |
|---|---|---|
| `print([["a"][0], 2])` | `['a', 2]` | refusal (Gap R.218's one-word message) |
| `print([[1.5, 2][0], 3])` | `[1.5, 3]` | refusal (same) |
| `xs = [1, "a"]` / `print([xs[1], 2])` | `['a', 2]` | refusal (a mixed list's element *is* a pair) |

so this row is one wrong answer and three missing halves. The fix is one hook: teach `pairElemPair` and
`nameIsPairElem` the subscript as well as the name, so a literal element that is itself a read arrives as the
`(payload, tag)` pair `heapListFromTagged` and `heapDictFrom` already know how to store — and keep the gates
that decide taggedness (`literalNeedsTags`, `taggableMixedList`, `elemTaggableOrPair`) asking the question the
builders ask. that last clause is ADR 0249's rule and the reason the row is written before the code: a gate
that admits what the door refuses, or refuses what the door admits, is how this fix would ship a refusal
nobody measured.

**Closed by ADR 0332 (2026-10-13), measured the same afternoon.** The hook grew the `*Index` arm beside the
`*Name` one and calls `taggedSlotPair` — the same call `print(xs[i])` emits — rather than a second read, so a
slot the builder wrote and the same slot the printer reads cannot mean different things. The gate is
`subscriptIsPairElem` in the new `pkg/lang/pair_element_read.go`: it emits nothing and asks the door's two
questions in the door's order (is the container side one the run time owns; is the read one the fold cannot
answer alone), and `isPairElem` — the union of "a name the pair road bound" and "a subscript the pair door
reads" — is now the question all three taggedness gates ask (`elemTaggableOrPair`, `literalHasPairElement`,
and through it the bit-8 "the slots describe themselves" claim). All four shapes answer the reference, and the
families that ride the same door came with them without extra work: a dict entry
(`print({1: {"a": "x"}["a"]})` was `{1: 1}`), a dict key (`print({{"a": "x"}["a"]: 1})` was `{1: 1}`), a set
member (was `{1}`), a container slot of a container the program built (`xs = []` / `xs.append([7, 8])` /
`print([xs[0][1], 0])` was refused outright), a dict *variable* read into a slot
(`xs = {"a": "x"}` / `print([xs["a"], 2])` was `[1, 2]`), and `print([str(x) …])`-free re-reads of the list
the element landed in (`len`, subscript, `in`, `for`, `str`, `repr`, `==`).

Two negative controls carry as much weight as the answers. The fold's shapes allocate nothing and call none of
the object doors — asserted over `@main` alone, because the runtime library legitimately calls `rt_get_elem`.
And one refusal stayed a refusal: `[id({"a": "x"}["a"]), 1]` hands a callee one `i32` and has nowhere to put a
register, so it names the missing half (Gap R.146) rather than joining the payload road. The row was watched
for exactly the inversion — a refusal relaxed to keep a suite green — and a guard asserts it still refuses.

Measured on the way, and **filed rather than bundled**: Gaps **R.225**, **R.226** and **R.227** below, plus
one shape that changed road rather than being fixed — `def f(): return [{"a": "x"}["a"], 2]` used to stop the
build with the static-array sentence and now prints `0`, which is **Gap R.67**'s road (`return [1, 2]` emits
`ret i32 @.lst1`; `la = [1, 2]; return la` prints `0`) arrived at from a new direction.

<a id="gap-r-225"></a>
### Gap R.225 — a literal element that is an *operation over* a read still answers the payload (OPEN, found by ADR 0332)

```python
print([str({"a": "x"}["a"]), 1])   # exit 0, prints [1, 1]; the reference prints ['x', 1]
print([{"a": "x"}["a"] + "!", 1])  # exit 0, prints [3, 1]; the reference prints ['x!', 1]
xs = [1, "a"]
print([str(xs[1]), 1])             # exit 0, prints [0, 1]; the reference prints ['a', 1]
d = {"a": "x"}
print([d["a"].upper(), 1])         # exit 0, prints [2, 1]; the reference prints ['X', 1]
```

ADR 0332 taught the builder to ask the pair door for an element that *is* a subscript. An element that merely
*contains* one is lowered by the ordinary road, which asks the subscript for one word — the read's payload —
and the container then labels the slot from the *expression's* apparent kind (`printsAsInternedStr` says
"text", which is true of the answer and useless for the word stored). The `@str_tab` position of `"x"` is `1`;
the slot says `int`; the printer obliges.

The gate's question is therefore one step short of the whole question: it asks about the element, not about
the element's operands. Widening it means answering "does *any* operand of this expression denote a pair?"
per operator and per call — and where the answer's kind cannot be labelled at all, refusing rather than
tagging it from the spelling, which is what makes this a separate row from R.224 and not a loose end of it.
The shapes are pinned with both answers written into
`TestWhatThePairElementDoorStillCannotReachIsFiledNotFixed`, so the day the door grows, a test fails loudly
instead of a wrong answer shipping quietly.

<a id="gap-r-226"></a>
### Gap R.226 — the loop that unrolls a literal binds the payload, not the value (OPEN, found by ADR 0332)

```python
for v in [{"a": "x"}["a"], 2]:   # prints 1 then 2; the reference prints x then 2
    print(v)
```

The same literal bound first prints correctly — `ys = [{"a": "x"}["a"], 2]` / `for v in ys:` — because that is
ADR 0185's loop: it walks the object and fetches `rt_get_elem` *and* `rt_tag_of` into `%_v` and `%_v_tag`. The
direct form is not a loop at all. `for` over a literal is unrolled, and each element expression is stored into
the loop variable through the one-word road, so the register the pair door computed never reaches the variable
and `print(v)` reads the integer road. Emitted IR says it plainly: a `store i32 %t8, i32* %_v` with no store
beside it into `%_v_tag`.

The fix is the unrolled binding asking `isPairElem` and storing both words — the pair, in the same
block, at both words — or ceasing to unroll a literal whose element the pair door answers. Until then the
bound form is the road that works, and the conformance program uses it (an honest `match`) while this row and
a filed-not-fixed row carry the direct form.

<a id="gap-r-227"></a>
### Gap R.227 — a subscript whose base is itself a subscript of a literal refuses (OPEN, found by ADR 0332)

```python
print([[1, 2][0][0], 1])   # exit 1: codegen: index requires an inline list/dict/set literal
print([[1][0][0], 1])      # the reference raises TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable
```

The fold answers the inner read — every element is an integer constant, the position is an integer — and the
outer subscript is then holding a base that is no longer a literal, so the subscript road's own gate condemns
it. The run-time door is never consulted, because the shape *started* from a literal and the roads are chosen
by the base's spelling rather than by what the compiler actually still holds.

Gap R.214 measured this at a call (`def build(): return [1, 2]` / `print(build()[7])`); this is the same
missing half one level in, and the same cure: hand the outer subscript the (payload, tag) pair the inner read
computed and let `slotReadUnderTag` ask the object what the payload is, which is exactly what ADR 0251 does for
a container the program built. The reference does not refuse these two and does not answer them: it raises, so
the definition of done is a trap at exit 3 with the reference's own sentence, catchable, and no `codegen:`
sentence anywhere in the output.

<a id="gap-r-228"></a>

### Gap R.228 — a `None` handed back by a function answers the digit `0` (CLOSED by ADR 0368, found by ADR 0333)

**Closed 2026-10-17 by ADR 0368.** The cure was the shape this section asked for — one whole-program scan, a
verdict only where every road agrees — with one change of plan: the scan does not answer "is this body's answer
the void", it answers "**how many kinds can this body hand back?**", and a body that can hand back more than one
carries the kind of the arm that ran. `def f(): return None` is one arm; `def f(x): if x: return 7` is two (the
`7` and the fall-off), and it is the second case the one-word road could never answer — the payload of a value
whose kind nothing recorded, printed with `%d`. The word stored is the tag table's own (`TagNone` is `3`, and
`pairTagNone` is the same digit, which `pkg/lang/answer_kind_test.go::TestTheAnswerKindWordsAreTheTagTable` holds
the two to), the store goes into the global the pair road already declared, and the print door reads the pair
rather than the payload. `print(f())` writes `None`; `def f(x): if x: return 7` writes `7` and `None`; and the
same body's `True`/`2` and `{'k': 1}`/`3` arms arrive as bool and dict rather than as `1` and a slot number.

What this row's own text said it would take — a void-specific table and a void-specific printer decision —
turned out to be a narrower version of the same missing record, and building the wider one cost nothing extra: the
container table's rule ("decline a body whose arms are not all one kind") is kept by the new scan too, and the
void's arm joins the other arms rather than owning a table of its own. Gap R.103's warning stands, and is honoured
the same way: the scan declines a kind it cannot spell out of the source rather than guessing, so a `print(f())`
that still answers digits has a named cause and a row (Gap R.324) rather than a plausible number.

<a id="gap-r-229"></a>

### Gap R.229 — a container answer is not yet a value at the element door or the method door (OPEN, found by ADR 0333)

```python
def build():
    return [1, 2]

print([build(), 3])          # [[1, 2], 3] in the reference;  refuses here
print(build().append(3))     # None in the reference;           refuses here
```

ADR 0333 gave the answer — a heap handle and a recorded kind — and eight roads consume it: print,
`str`/`repr`/f-string, `len`, `in`, `not`, truthiness, a loop iterable, `==`, a binding. Two neighbours of
those roads stop one position earlier, and they are different owners:

- **The element door.** ADR 0332 taught the container builder to take a *subscript* as a (payload, tag)
  pair. A **call** that answers a container is the same situation — the compiler knows the kind and the
  builder has a register for it — and `isPairElem` does not ask about calls, so the element is lowered by
  the one-word road and the position has nowhere to put the kind. The refusal is honest and it is the right
  shape: the fix is to hand the answer's (handle, kind) to `rt_tag_elem` exactly as a read's pair goes.
- **The slice door** (joined 2026-10-14 by ADR 0334). `print(b()[0:2])` over a container the callee built
  refuses with ADR 0333's one-word sentence, and the row's decision is to leave it refused: the road it would
  land on is broken for every base — `print(ys[0:2])` of a mixed list answers `[1, 0]`, and binding a slice
  answers `1` (**Gap R.230**, which owns the tags the copy drops). Rewriting the answer into that road would
  have bought one more silently-wrong program at exit 0 for one honest refusal at exit 1. The `*Slice` arm of
  `containerAnswerSubscript` is written when R.230 pays, and its two test rows are already in place.
- **The method door.** `build().append(3)` needs the receiver materialised before dispatch, and the method
  road chooses its receiver from a name or a literal. Gap R.154 owns the parameter half of the same
  question (`takes(build())` where `takes` is `len(xs)`), and this is the receiver half: the road that
  already has a container in hand will not look inside a call for one.

Both rows carry the reference's answer beside this backend's refusal in
`TestWhatTheContainerAnswerStillCannotReachIsFiledNotFixed`, and both name the door rather than the value,
which is the distinction that makes them two owners instead of one: the value exists, and each door has to
grow an arm to reach it.

<a id="gap-r-219"></a>
### Gap R.219 — a function is registered as returning text on the evidence of one arm (CLOSED by ADR 0368, found by ADR 0327)

**Closed 2026-10-17 by ADR 0368** — answering the shape this row asked us to refuse, and four more it did
not name: `ys.append(f(1))`, `s.add(f(1))`, `d["k"] = f(1)` and `ys[0] = f(1)` over a body whose arms mix kinds
were refused outright (*cannot put `f(...)` in a compiled list: the compiler cannot prove one kind for it*), and
all four now answer the reference — `['a']`, `{'a'}`, `{'k': 'a'}`, `['a']` — because the three gates that decide
whether a literal or a mutation needs per-element tags learned that an answer carrying its own kind is such an
element (ADR 0249's rule about a gate and a door that disagree, read the other way: the door grew and the gate
had to follow). The row's own plan was to
register a function as text-returning only where *every* reachable return is text-valued and to refuse the mixed
body; the reason to prefer answering it is that the refusal is unnecessary once the answer carries its kind, and the
refusal would have cost programs the reference runs (`while f():`, `print(f(0))`) their one green leg. So
`textReturningCallables` and `scanStringBindings` now ask one question before writing `strFuncs`: *does the answer
direction carry this body?* A body whose arms all answer one kind is registered exactly as it always was — the
table is correct for it, and `TestACarriedAnswerIsVisibleInTheEmittedModule` fails if a one-kind body is handed a
kind word it does not need. A body whose arms answer two kinds gets **no entry**, because an entry is a claim about
a single payload and there is no longer a single payload.

The measurement that says the change is real: of a 25-shape probe of mixed-return bodies, **12 changed answer and
none regressed** — the same probe run against a build of the parent commit prints 19 wrong. Root cause, in one
sentence: `returnsStringExpr`/`methodReturnsStr` set `strFuncs` when *any* return yielded text, and the caller then
handed `printf` an interned `@str_tab` index with `%d` for the arm that answered a number.

Two rules were learned the hard way and are written into the scan rather than into a comment. The first is ADR
0343's: the scan answers *to its caller* and is not left in a package variable, so two compiles in flight cannot be
answered by one plan — `TestAnswerKindPlanIsNotAPackageVariable` keeps that honest. The second is ADR 0273's, and
it is the difference between a gate and a trap: seeding the pair road's `pairRetDone` from the answer direction turns
every arithmetic, comparison and call-argument position of a mixed body into an exit-1 refusal, which is what the
first attempt did and what `value`'s gate now refuses to do (`!g.answer.carries(name)` is that exemption, with the
reasoning in the comment above it). Those doors still read a bare payload; they are Gap R.324, filed the same day
rather than smoothed over, and they are why this row's definition of done is not simply "everything agrees".

<a id="gap-r-220"></a>
### Gap R.220 — a dict read handed to a call answers the payload, not the value (OPEN, found by ADR 0327)

```

def id(v):
    return v

print(id(d["a"]))     # exit 0, prints 1 — the text's @str_tab index; the reference prints x
print(id({"a": "x"}["a"]))  # exit 1: refuses, naming the pair, the one word and Gap R.146
```

Gap R.146's one-word position measured from the dict side: the read produces a `(payload, tag)` pair and the
